consensus_summary: The blind consensus treats 'stranger' as a multi-stranded symbol with two dominant streams: (1) the vulnerable outsider to be welcomed, in whom Christ is encountered (Matt 25:35; Lev 19:33-34; Heb 13:2), and (2) the believer as pilgrim/sojourner whose true home is heaven (Heb 11:13; 1 Pet 2:11). A widely listed third stream is alienation from God's covenant, resolved in Christ (Eph 2:12, 19) — this is even the primary meaning in Response C. Minority readings include the false shepherd (John 10:5) and Christ as unrecognized stranger.
book_summary: The book defines the stranger as a non-citizen of God's commonwealth: one outside the covenant who may be drawn in, and who, once brought in, becomes in turn a stranger to the world. It anchors this exclusively in Ephesians 2:12, 19, framing the symbol around covenant citizenship status rather than hospitality ethics.
consensus_core_identification: An outsider figure with two chief symbolic uses: the marginalized person owed hospitality (in whom Christ is met) and the believer as heavenly-citizen sojourning on earth, with covenant alienation (Eph 2) as a recognized common strand.
book_core_identification: One alienated from God's covenant commonwealth — a spiritual non-citizen — who upon incorporation reverses status and becomes a stranger to the world instead.
boundary_disagreement: The book elevates the Ephesians 2 covenant-alienation strand (a common alternative in Responses A/B/D, primary in C) to the sole core, and fuses it with the pilgrim motif as its converse ('once in, made a stranger to the world'). It thereby drops the hospitality/vulnerable-outsider strand (Matt 25, Lev 19, Heb 13:2) that most consensus responses treat as dominant or co-dominant, and excludes literal social-category strangers (resident aliens owed protection) from the symbol's extension.
rationale: The book's core is recognizably within the consensus map — covenant alienation via Eph 2:12, 19 is explicitly listed by all four responses and is Response C's primary meaning; the 'stranger to the world' clause mirrors the pilgrim stream in B and D. So there is no replaced referent or contradiction. However, the book materially reorganizes the symbol: it makes covenant citizenship the single organizing idea, treats the pilgrim identity as the post-conversion inversion of the same status, and silently excludes the hospitality/ethical reading that the consensus regards as at least co-primary. That is a real boundary change within a preserved category — REFINED, not MATCH.
strongest_objection: One could argue MATCH: every element of the book's definition (covenant alienation and believer-as-stranger-to-the-world) appears in the consensus responses, and Response C even makes the Eph 2 reading primary, so the difference could be seen as mere emphasis rather than a material boundary change. Additionally, the printed citations fully support the covenant-alienation half, arguably making support STRONG for the entry's main claim.
